REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT OF

THE
HONOURABLE MADAM JUSTICE FRUMAN

____________________________________________________

[
1
]

To express his anger against the Jewish community for events in the
Middle East, Yousef Sandouga hurled a Molotov cocktail at an Edmonton
synagogue, setting it on fire. He pled guilty to arson, under
s. 434
of the
Criminal
Code
, and was sentenced to a 12-month gaol term, and three years’
probation. The crown appealed the sentence, asking for a two and one-half to
three-year penitentiary term. Sandouga also appealed, asking for a reduction in
his sentence.

BACKGROUND

[
2
]

The incident occurred at approximately 12:50 a.m. on November 1, 2000.
Sandouga, dressed in dark clothing and a black toque, assembled two Molotov
cocktails by filling glass bottles with gasoline and attaching a wick. He lit
one and threw it at the Beth Shalom Synagogue, breaking a window. Although the
Molotov cocktail did not enter the building, it set fire to the east wall.
While attempting to light the second Molotov cocktail, Sandouga inadvertently
set his own clothing on fire. He rolled on the ground to extinguish the flames,
dropping his cell phone. These actions aroused the attention of the synagogue
caretaker, who lived in a residence immediately adjacent to the east side of
the synagogue. She saw the offender flee, and discovered his cell phone.

[
3
]

The caretaker's son began fighting the fire with water and a bucket. The
emergency response department arrived within minutes and extinguished the
blaze. As a result of their speedy response, the damage was confined to
scorched bricks, burned vegetation and two broken windows. Fire investigators found
the second Molotov cocktail discarded on the ground. They also found gasoline
spread along the east side of the synagogue, indicating an intent to cause a
larger fire.

[
4
]

The police arrived promptly and recovered the cell phone. They soon
received a number of angry and threatening phone calls. One caller identified
the cell phone as Sandouga’s, and provided his address for its return. The
police contacted the phone’s registered owner and determined that it had been
in Sandouga’s possession at the time of the incident. They also learned that
Sandouga had been treated for second-degree burns at the Royal Alex Hospital
shortly after 2:00 a.m. on the morning of the fire. With the assistance of
“elders in the Arabic community” in Edmonton, Sandouga was located the
following day (AB 5). He turned himself in to the police late that afternoon.

[
5
]

Sandouga gave a cautioned statement to the police in which he admitted
setting fire to the synagogue. He indicated that he had been drinking that
evening and was acting alone. According to the agreed facts, “[o]ut of
frustration with events in the Middle East [Sandouga] decided to act out
against the local Jewish community. Sandouga claims relatives and friends of
his family lost their lives in the Middle East conflict and the pressures are
being felt here” (AB 6).

[
6
]

Sandouga was born in Jordan, and emigrated to Canada when he was 7. He
returned to live in Jordan between the ages of 14 and 17. He considers himself
and his family to be Palestinians. He has no criminal record, and was 20 years
old at the time of the offence. With the involvement of elders in his
community, he met with representatives of the synagogue. Restitution of
approximately $1100 for damages was paid, although it is not clear from the
record whether Sandouga himself paid it. Sandouga served no time in custody
prior to being sentenced.

[
7
]

The sentencing judge accepted Sandouga’s guilty plea to arson. He
characterized Sandouga’s crime as an act of terrorism and extremism, and
indicated that Sandouga’s actions had destroyed the “community of Edmonton”. He
contemplated whether a conditional sentence might be appropriate, but concluded
that “this conduct is so horrible [...] that a gaol term has to be imposed” (AB
51-52). He considered Sandouga’s age, guilty plea, his efforts to make
reparations and the burns he suffered, then imposed a 12-month gaol term,
followed by three years’ probation, with Sandouga to take treatment as directed
by the probation officer (AB 53).

[
8
]

The sentencing judge made a number of errors in principle. His
misappreciation of the degree of Sandouga’s moral culpability, failure to
consider serious aggravating circumstances, and lack of emphasis on
denunciation and general deterrence in sentencing for a terrorist act all
contributed to the imposition of a sentence that was demonstrably unfit.

MORAL CULPABILITY

[
9
]

The judge found Sandouga’s conduct to be reprehensible but concluded
that there was no “moral turpitude” (AB 52). He added:

I accept, and there is no reason
for me not to accept, your version that you were drinking that evening, that
this was an act, perhaps not of revenge, but of, as your counsel said, of
anger, not intended to be terrorism or extremism. But it was. That is what it
turned out to be.

[
10
]

Property destruction resulting from an impulsive act of anger generally
involves less culpability than a planned and deliberate act of revenge. The
sentencing judge characterized Sandouga’s crime as an act of anger, but failed
to appreciate that it was also motivated by revenge against the Jewish
community for incidents that had taken place in Palestine. An excerpt from
Sandouga’s statement to the police, which was entered as an agreed fact,
included Sandouga’s confirmation that the firebombing was motivated by revenge
(AB 9). But even without this admission, the facts support no other conclusion.
“Revenge” is defined as “the act of doing hurt or harm to another in return for
wrong or injury suffered”:
The Oxford English Dictionary,
2d ed.,
s.v.

“revenge”
. Because Sandouga’s planned attack on an Edmonton synagogue
was in retaliation for events in Palestine, he acted out of revenge.

[
11
]

The fundamental sentencing principle is that “a sentence must be
proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of
the offender” (s. 718.1). As a result of his failure to appreciate Sandouga’s
revenge-based motive for the crime, the sentencing judge undervalued his degree
of moral responsibility.

[
12
]

There are other indicia of Sandouga’s culpability. This incident
involved considerably more advance planning and deliberation than is
characteristic of an outburst of anger resulting from alcohol consumption.
First, Sandouga assembled the necessary equipment: earlier in the day he went
to a gas station to procure a jerry can of gasoline, and collected glass
bottles and wicks. Second, he located a synagogue. Third, he dressed in dark
clothing and a toque. Fourth, he drove to the synagogue, using his father’s
car. Fifth, he waited until 12:50 a.m., when he could perform his attack under
cover of darkness. In addition, in his statement to the police, Sandouga
admitted that he discussed the proposed firebombing with a number of people.
All of them attempted to dissuade him from carrying it out, but he refused to
heed their advice (AB 12-13).

[
13
]

Despite his guilty plea, Sandouga is unwilling to accept full
responsibility for his behaviour. According to the presentence report, Sandouga
claimed “it was not really me who did it” because he’d consumed alcohol and
used marijuana that evening. He also denied that his actions were planned,
asserting that “the idea just came to me” (AB E19).

[
14
]

The extent of the intended damage also supports a finding of substantial
culpability. The minimal damage to the synagogue was not a result of Sandouga’s
restraint. He fully intended to lob the second Molotov cocktail through the
window he had already broken, to set fire to the interior of the building. He
would have done so had he not set himself on fire in the process. He also
poured gasoline along the east wall of the synagogue, which, had it ignited,
would have contributed to a larger blaze. The use of such an accelerant
increases the risks to firefighters. In addition, the occupants of the
caretaker’s residence adjacent to the east side of the synagogue were at
considerable risk.

[
15
]

The revenge-based motive for the crime, the degree of planning and
deliberation, and the extent of the intended destruction all indicate
significant culpability. The sentencing judge erred by failing to appreciate
the extent of Sandouga’s moral responsibility.

AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCES

[
16
]

A court is required, in imposing a sentence, to consider aggravating and
mitigating circumstances (s. 718.2(a)). Aggravating circumstances must be
established by proof beyond a reasonable doubt (s. 724(3)(e)). Section
718.2(a)(i) addresses hate crimes. It deems “evidence that the offence was
motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on race, national or ethnic origin,
[...] religion, [...] or any other similar factor [...] to be [an] aggravating
[circumstance]”. The word “motivated” implies a link between the bias,
prejudice or hate and the decision to commit the crime.

[
17
]

In his statement to the police, Sandouga indicated that he does not hate
Jews. However, his decision to firebomb a synagogue was not random. According
to the agreed facts, Sandouga decided to act out against the local Jewish
community (AB 6). His counsel conceded that Sandouga’s actions were “an
expression of anger directed against the Jewish community because of events on
the other side of the world” (AB 50).

[
18
]

Sandouga’s actions were directed against an identifiable religious group
and were motivated by revenge against all members of that group. Sandouga
targeted the synagogue because its congregants are adherents of the same
religion as the people he considers responsible for problems in Palestine.
There is a clear link between his enmity towards or prejudice against the
Jewish people, and his commission of the crime. The offence is therefore a hate
crime. The sentencing judge erred in principle by failing to consider this
serious aggravating circumstance.

[
19
]

The target of Sandouga’s attack, a synagogue, is another aggravating
circumstance. He attempted to destroy a place of worship, the visible symbol of
a religion, traditionally a place of devotion, sanctuary, peace and safety for
its adherents. It is immaterial whether the building was a temple, a mosque, a
church, a cathedral or a synagogue. An attempt to destroy a place of worship
intimidates and engenders fear among adherents, limiting the way they exercise
their religious freedom. Such actions undermine freedom of religion, a value
Canadians cherish, and erode a fundamental freedom guaranteed by the
Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
(s. 2(a)).

[
20
]

Sandouga’s counsel submits that his crime is less serious because
Sandouga’s intent was not to intimidate the local Jewish community or to force
its members to act in a particular way. This contention finds no support in the
agreed facts or the presentence report. Nothing in this record suggests
Sandouga did not intend the foreseeable and logical consequences of his
actions.

[
21
]

Intimidation of the Edmonton Jewish community was certainly one of
those  consequences. The trial judge found that the community had been
“terrorized” (AB 51). A victim impact statement prepared on behalf of the
synagogue noted “tremendous anxiety expressed and felt by our congregants due
to this incident” (AB E14). The synagogue purchased security systems at its
members’ expense, hired security guards, locked doors it had never locked
before, heightened security procedures, and increased monitoring and vigilance.
Congregants continue to be concerned about a repeat incident.

[
22
]

Even with the greatest security precautions, everyone who frequents a
place of worship that has been targeted and firebombed, and perhaps every
adherent of the same religion, would feel uneasy about their personal safety.
Sandouga committed a dangerous and unlawful act of religious intimidation that
has a widespread and profound effect. His actions detrimentally alter the way
in which all adherents of the Jewish religion gather to worship.

[
23
]

Nor is the Edmonton Jewish community the only one to be harmed.
Sandouga’s destructive action has damaged the reputation of his own community.
The synagogue’s victim impact statement at E14 noted:

Because the accused and now
convicted vandal was from the Arab community it caused more stress on the
already troubled relationship that is in place between our respective groups.
This incident set back some of the progress that has been made and only through
the dogged determination and efforts of community leaders has there been
renewed cooperation.

[
24
]

This is yet another unfortunate consequence of hate crimes: they affect
community perception of the group the perpetrator purports to represent,
inviting stereotyping, suspicion and mistrust. Such crimes encourage disharmony
among religious groups and disruption in community relationships, at a time
when communication and understanding are most needed.

DENUNCIATION AND GENERAL DETERRENCE

[
25
]

Sandouga, for a political purpose, targeted and intimidated a religious
group by firebombing their place of worship. The sentencing judge correctly
characterized his crime as an act of terrorism, but erred by failing to
emphasize denunciation and general deterrence in imposing a sentence.

[
26
]

Terrorist acts take on a special public dimension because of the
importance Canadians place on multiculturalism. We welcome immigrants from
diverse nations, and encourage them to retain their heritage and distinct
cultural identities, a policy enshrined in
s. 27
of the
Charter
.
With
this privilege comes the corresponding obligation to respect the dignity and cultural
identity of others. Canada does not punish people for their political beliefs
or social values, as long as they are expressed in lawful ways. But our
tolerance ends when political ideology manifests itself in terrorist acts,
involving violence to others or destruction of their property.

[
27
]

Unfortunately, acts of terrorism have broad repercussions. They are
rarely isolated incidents, but “invite imitation and repetition by others, and
incite retaliation”:
R.
v.
Ingram and Grimsdale

(1977),
1977 CanLII 2018 (ON CA)
, 35
C.C.C. (2d) 376 at 379 (Ont. C.A.). Such actions therefore threaten the fabric
of Canada’s multicultural, pluralistic society. See
R.
v.
Soles,

[1998] O.J. No. 5061
, online: Q.L. (O.J.) at para. 20 (Gen. Div.);
R.
v
.
Lelas
(1990),
1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
, 58 C.C.C. (3d) 568 at 574-75 (Ont. C.A.);
Ingram
and Grimsdale
,
supra
, at 379. Because these repugnant activities
must be discouraged, the primary objectives in imposing a sentence for a
terrorist act are denunciation and general deterrence.

[
28
]

This sentencing principle appears consistently in cases involving
violent acts of terrorism. The sentence “must be one which expresses the public
abhorrence for such conduct and their refusal to countenance it”:
Ingram
and Grimsdale
,
supra
, at 379. When an offence “involves a
violent act of international terrorism performed in a country unconnected with
the place in which the alleged injustices have been perpetrated, the need for
an unusually strong general deterrent prevails”:
R.
v
. Balian

(1988), 29 O.A.C. 387 at 389 (C.A.)
. In sentencing for acts of terrorism,
“deterrence must be considered to be of paramount importance. The sentence
imposed must be sufficient to bring home to others contemplating a similar
terrorist act that this type of conduct will not be tolerated, nor will it be
treated lightly by the courts”:
R.
v.
Atwal
(1990),
1990 CanLII 10930 (BC CA)
, 57
C.C.C. (3d) 143 at 145 (B.C.C.A.), quoting Callaghan J.’s unreported trial
decision. “Conduct fostered by philosophies and beliefs that condone and extol
violence as a means of disapproval of those perceived to be in opposition to
those philosophies and beliefs must be sternly denounced by the courts”:
R.

v.
Simms
(1990),
1990 ABCA 352 (CanLII)
, 60 C.C.C. (3d) 499 at 507 (Alta. C.A.).

[
29
]

The same emphasis on denunciation and general deterrence applies to hate
crimes directed against property. In
Lelas
,
supra
, the
offender spray-painted Nazi and anti-Semitic slogans and symbols on a
synagogue. The court stated at 575 that “[t]he message must go out loud and
clear that conduct, such as that engaged in by the respondent, will not be
tolerated in Canadian society, and if it is engaged in, it will be met with a
severe penalty.” In
Soles
,
supra
, the offender knocked
over 43 headstones in a Jewish cemetery. The court concluded at para. 24 that
the sentence had to “reflect society’s abhorrence of this type of hate crime”.

[
30
]

The emphasis on denunciation and deterrence also applies to terrorist
acts resulting in property destruction that are not classified as hate crimes.
In
R.
v.
Bettger
,
[1995] N.W.T.J. No. 88
, online: Q.L.
(N.W.T.J.) (Sup. Ct.), two members of a striking mine-workers’ union
spray-painted anti-scab slogans on equipment, stole explosives and set off two
explosions in the mine. The court indicated at para. 23 that “general
deterrence and denunciation are the over-riding factors.” In
R.
v.

Thurston
(1994), 149 A.R. and 63 W.A.C. 226, an animal rights activist
set fires at a fish company, and broke into and vandalized a university kennel,
releasing 29 cats. This court stated at 228:

A free society cannot survive
when zealots [...] deliberately break the law in an effort to impose their will
on others by dangerous and unlawful intimidation. When they do, the court has
an obligation to impose an exemplary sentence to recognize the serious nature
of the crimes and to deter others from seeking to achieve their private ends
through similar illegal means.

[
31
]

Sandouga’s crime involved not only a terrorist act, but a hate crime and
an act of religious intimidation. Such crimes chip away at our human dignity,
our fundamental freedoms, our multicultural tolerance, and our sense of safety
and security. All Canadians are entitled to live, gather and worship without
fear of attack. To protect these shared values, to discourage anarchy, and to
maintain confidence in the judicial system, courts must mete out penalties that
sternly denounce hate crimes and terrorist acts, and deter others from
expressing their views through dangerous acts of intimidation.

A FIT SENTENCE

[
32
]

The maximum sentence for arson is 14 years, indicating that Parliament
considers this to be a serious crime. While a particular sentence always
depends on the circumstances of the offence and the offender, in determining a
fit sentence, it is customary to consider sentences in similar cases.

[
33
]

The case law suggests that planned, revenge-based acts of destruction of
another person’s property generally attract a substantial sentence. For
example, in
R.
v.
Etmannski
(2001),
2001 ABPC 90 (CanLII)
, 294 A.R. 344 (Prov. Ct.),
the offender, to “get back” at her boyfriend’s former girlfriend, threw Molotov
cocktails through a window of the girlfriend’s residence, creating a small fire
that was rapidly extinguished. There was little damage and no injury. The
accused was 19, pled guilty and had been encouraged by her boyfriend to commit
the arson. She had a criminal record, mostly in youth court, with 4 months’
closed custody as her longest previous sentence. Etmannski was sentenced to 27
months, in addition to 4 months’ pretrial custody. See also
R.
v.

Wattenberger
(1984),
1984 ABCA 240 (CanLII)
, 56 A.R. 238 (C.A.) (grain elevator employee
angered by employer’s refusal to allow him time off set fire to grain elevator;
sentence of three years);
R.
v.
Sillars
(18 April 1990),
Edmonton 9003-0237A6 (C.A.)

(lumber company employee whose
employment was terminated set fire to lumber company both for revenge and to
conceal his theft of $240; guilty plea; effective sentence of three years, with
credit for pretrial custody); and
R.
v.
Allard
,
[1999]
B.C.J. No. 1912
, online: Q.L. (B.C.J.) (C.A.) (offender set fire to residence
after he was told to leave by his cohabitant; effective sentence of four years,
with credit for pretrial custody).

[
34
]

Revenge-based property destruction with a terrorist or urban
intimidation aspect pushes the sentence even higher. Because of the emphasis on
denunciation and general deterrence, these crimes consistently attract
penitentiary terms, despite strong mitigating circumstances. For example, in
Bettger
,

supra
, the mine explosion case, both offenders pled guilty, had no prior
record, had families they supported and were not at risk to reoffend. The court
imposed a sentence of three years on one offender and two and one-half years on
the other, in addition to eight months’ pretrial custody. In
Thurston
,

supra
, the animal rights activism case, the offender pled guilty, was
23, had no prior criminal record, had renounced his unlawful methods and was
not perceived to be a threat to the public. The court imposed a sentence of two
years less a day, in addition to 15 months’ pretrial custody, noting at 229
that it did not intend to convey the impression that this is the maximum
sentence “the court is prepared to impose in cases of dangerous and unlawful
public intimidation.”

[
35
]

The mitigating circumstances in this case include Sandouga’s youth and
lack of a prior criminal record. He pled guilty, but accepted only “partial
responsibility for his behaviour and expressed some remorse” (AB E23).
Restitution was paid, although it is not clear whether Sandouga himself paid
it. The presentence report concludes that because of the nature of the offence,
Sandouga may pose a threat to the community (AB E23). Unlike
Bettger
,

supra
, and
Thurston
, supra
, the sentencing judge
did not find that Sandouga was not at risk to reoffend or was not a continuing
threat to the community.

[
36
]

Sandouga’s counsel contends that his crime is less serious because
Sandouga acted alone. A terrorist act does not require membership in an
international terrorist organization or an extremist political group.  While
such an affiliation might be an aggravating factor, a lack of group support in
no way detracts from the nature or seriousness of Sandouga’s crime or the
extent of his culpability.

[
37
]

A one-year sentence would be at the low end of the sentencing spectrum
for arson in retaliation for a private grievance. Sandouga’s act of
revenge-based arson was a terrorist act, a hate crime and an act of religious
intimidation. The one-year sentence imposed by the judge in this case is
demonstrably unfit. The mitigating circumstances do not outweigh the need to
denounce Sandouga’s actions, and to unequivocally indicate that such hate
crimes and terrorist acts will not be countenanced.

[
38
]

The crown’s appeal is allowed. Sandouga is sentenced to two and one-half
years’ imprisonment in a federal penitentiary. Sandouga’s appeal is dismissed.

[
39
]

Because crimes of this nature encompass a broad range of conduct, this
judgment is not intended to establish a starting point sentence for hate crimes
and terrorist acts directed against property.
